title: Treatment of sugar processing industry effluent up to remittance limits: Suitability of hybrid electrode for electrochemical reactor
author: Sahu
materials: The complete experimental is shown in Fig. 1. The manageable electrochemical container was prepared from transparent glass and fitted with a pair of anode and cathode. These electrodes were arranged in parallel and maintained 20 mm space between them. A DC power was supply through electrodes. The current supply and voltage were measured with ammeter and voltmeter. The electrochemical reactor was used for batch and continuous experiments. The configuration of the reactor is given in Table 2. When a potential (usually of direct current) is applied from an external power source, the anode material undergoes oxidation, while the cathode will be subjected to reduction or reductive deposition of elemental metals. The thermogravitmetry analysis (TGA), differential thermogravitmetry analysis (DTGA) and derivative thermal analysis (DTA) of scrum sludge and supernaent dried mass thermal characteristics was studied. Fig. 9 (a) and (b) shows DTG, DTA, and TG curve of the scum and precipitated sludge obtained at pH 6.5. TG curve shows that up to 300 °C temperature, dehydration and volatilization (reduction of volatiles) of the sample takes place and a reduction of 20 μg wt% and 17.2 μg wt% is recorded for scum and sludge respectively. From 300 °C to 600 °C, in the span of 300 °C, the precipitate is oxidized, losing about 8.4 wt% of scum and 4.6 wt% of the sludge. After 600 °C the oxidation is slow and the final decrease in weight of the scum and sludge is recorded as 6.5 wt% and 3.5 wt% respectively. The ash in scum and sludge remains 65.1% and 74.7%. The DTG curve shows the peak rate of weight loss of 87 μg min−1 at 140 °C for sludge and 120 μg min−1 at 113 °C for scum. The oxidation of top scum is exothermic, with a heat evolution of 230 MJ kg−1 at 400 °C. This study shows the inorganic nature of the sludge.Fig. 9Thermal analysis (DTG, DTA and TG) of (a) scum and (b) sludge.Fig. 9

steps.title: Assemble electrochemical reactor
steps.instruction: Use a transparent Perspex glass container (dimensions 10.7 × 10.7 × 13.74 cm, volume 1.55 dm³) and place a magnetic stir bar inside; the reactor will be operated in batch mode.

steps.title: Install parallel iron‑aluminium electrodes
steps.instruction: Prepare rectangular (square) plates of iron‑aluminium, size 8 cm × 8 cm, thickness 2 mm. Position the anode and cathode parallel to each other with a 20 mm (2 cm) gap, giving an effective electrode surface area of 64 cm². Connect each electrode to the ammeter and voltmeter leads.

steps.title: Add effluent sample to reactor
steps.instruction: Fill the reactor with the sugar‑processing industry effluent up to the container capacity (≈1.55 L) and start magnetic stirring to obtain a homogeneous mixture.

steps.title: Set power supply and apply DC potential
steps.instruction: Connect the electrodes to a DC power supply capable of 0–30 V and 0–5 A. Set the desired voltage/current according to the experimental design and record the values with the voltmeter and ammeter.

steps.title: Conduct batch electrocoagulation run
steps.instruction: Maintain stirring and apply the selected DC potential for the predetermined treatment time (as defined in the experimental plan). Electrochemical reactions occurring are: (1) M(s) → Mⁿ⁺ + ne⁻ (anode oxidation); (2) 2 H₂O → 4 H⁺ + O₂ + 4e⁻ (water oxidation); (3) Mⁿ⁺ + ne⁻ → M(s) (cathode reduction); (4) 2 H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2 OH⁻ (hydrogen evolution).

steps.title: Collect samples and perform analytical measurements
steps.instruction: Stop the power supply, allow the slurry to settle, and filter to separate the clear filtrate from the sludge. Analyze the filtrate for: COD by the standard dichromate reflux method; chloride by the Volhard titration; sulfates and phosphates by standard methods; metal ions by atomic absorption spectroscopy (GBC Awanta, Australia). Determine protein content by the Bradford method and colour by UV–Vis spectrophotometry at λ = 475 nm (Perkin‑Elmer Lambda 35). Dry the sludge and carry out thermal analysis (TGA/DTG/DTA) using a Pyris Diamond analyzer (Perkin‑Elmer).
